# QR Test Fixtures

Design record for the committed fixture corpus and its generator (`tools/QRInteropFixtures`). It records what the corpus is, why it exists, and the external oracles it draws from. The testing strategy the corpus serves is recorded under [Why](#why) below.

---

## What

### Purpose

The corpus is a set of symbols produced by encoders **other than FeatherQR**. It is committed to the repository so that PR CI can check this library's decoder against independent implementations without needing external toolchains at test time.

It exists because round-trip tests alone cannot catch a bug that the encoder and the decoder share. If this library's encoder and decoder agree on the same mistake, round trips still pass. Fixtures generated by other encoders do not.

### Layout

```
tests/FeatherQR.Tests/Fixtures/
├── StandardQr/
│   └── zxing-net/              (one directory per generator)
│       ├── case-name.json       manifest
│       ├── case-name.matrix.txt core module matrix, '1' dark / '0' light, row-major, LF, no quiet zone
│       └── case-name.png        clean black-on-white render (quiet zone 4, 8 px/module)
├── StandardQrStructuredAppend/
│   ├── qrcodegenerator/        (same three files per symbol; one set = case-name-{index}of{count})
│   ├── codeglyphx/
│   └── zxing-cpp-samples/      (third-party captures: json + png only, no matrix; PROVENANCE.md + LICENSE beside them)
├── MicroQR/
│   ├── zint-libzint/           (same three files; PNG quiet zone 2 per the Micro QR spec)
│   └── qrtool/
├── RmQr/
│   ├── zint-libzint/           (same three files; rectangular matrix / PNG, quiet zone 2 per ISO/IEC 23941)
│   └── qrtool/
└── RealImages/
    └── zxing-cpp-samples/      (third-party photographs, scans and renders: image + .txt with its text, one directory per sample set; PROVENANCE.md + LICENSE beside them; measured by the image decode sweep, a few images pinned by the tests that read them)
```

### Manifest schema (case-name.json, camelCase)

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | Case name (= file stem) |
| `generator`, `generatorVersion` | Producing implementation and its pinned version |
| `symbolType` | `StandardQR`, `MicroQR` or `rMQR` |
| `version`, `width`, `height` | Symbol version and core module dimensions. For rMQR, `version` is the ISO/IEC 23941 version index + 1, which equals the `RmQRVersion` value and the libzint version number, and `width` ≠ `height` |
| `versionName` | Human-readable version, present only where the version is not a plain integer (rMQR: `R7x43`) |
| `errorCorrectionLevel` | `L` / `M` / `Q` / `H`, as requested (the generator honors the request) |
| `mode` | Data segment mode reported by the generator |
| `maskPattern` | Mask chosen by the generator, or `-1` when unknown. For Micro QR and rMQR the sanity gate takes it from the reader. rMQR is always `4`, its single mask expressed as a Standard QR pattern number |
| `payloadText`, `payloadUtf8Hex` | Expected decode result (text and UTF-8 bytes) |
| `eciCharset` | `UTF-8` when the generator was asked to emit an ECI segment, else null |
| `quietZoneModules`, `pixelsPerModule` | PNG render parameters (`0` for third-party captures, which are not renders) |
| `structuredAppend` | Present only on a symbol of a Structured Append set: `setId` (the case name), `index` (0-based, as on the wire), `count` (1..16) and `parity` (0..255). Every value is what the zxing-cpp reader reports for the symbol, never what the encoder was asked for |

The loader (`FixtureLoader` in the test project) mirrors this schema, so the two must change together.

`mode` is `Unknown` where no generator reports it: the Structured Append lineages and the third-party captures. The one exception is `Kanji`. The gate sets it when the bytes the set carries are the case text in Shift_JIS and no ECI header is present.

A Byte segment carrying raw Shift_JIS bytes without an ECI would look the same to the reader, because the reader exposes segment bytes, not modes. No Structured Append lineage writes such a segment. The gate refuses the other case it cannot name, an ECI header over ASCII-only bytes, rather than guess which ECI it was.

### Corpus contents (Standard QR, 28 cases)

The cases cover every mode (Numeric / Alphanumeric / Byte) × every ECC level at small versions. They add the version 1-L alphanumeric capacity boundary (25 chars), mid versions (v10/v15/v25), the maximum (v40-L at exactly 7089 digits), the full alphanumeric charset, and UTF-8/ECI payloads (Japanese, emoji).

Since the Kanji decode work there are also 7 Kanji-mode cases (ISO/IEC 18004 8.4.5). Two of them were added in Kanji encoding phase 6.6 for the 12-bit count band (versions 27-40): one character past version 26-M (653 at 27-M), and version 40-L filled (1,817). Both cycle through cells that include the edges of both Shift_JIS ranges (0x8140, 0x9FFC, 0xE040, 0xEAA4).

ZXing.Net emits Kanji mode when the requested charset is Shift_JIS and the payload is entirely JIS X 0208 double-byte. Its encoder reports `Mode.KANJI` itself, so the manifest mode is the generator's own report, not an assumption. ZXing.Net encodes through .NET CP932, so these payloads deliberately avoid the seven cells where CP932 and JIS X 0208 disagree. Those cells live in the qrtool rMQR lineage, which takes raw Shift_JIS bytes.

All payloads are fixed literals or fixed repetitions, with no randomness or timestamps, so regeneration is byte-reproducible for a given generator version.

### Corpus contents (Standard QR Structured Append, 7 sets × 2 lineages + 1 third-party set)

Two in-process encoder lineages each write seven sets, 95 symbols in all. The sets cover every mode (numeric, alphanumeric, byte), ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8 text, the smallest set (2, at version 1), the largest (16, at version 2), and set sizes in between at versions 3 to 9.

The two lineages differ in how they build a set:

- The `qrcodegenerator` lineage is a balancing encoder. It picks the count and a shared version itself, and boosts ECC per symbol: the version-1 pair comes out Q from a requested L, and the sixteen-set mixes L and M.
- The `codeglyphx` lineage takes the text pre-split into equal character runs and chooses each symbol's version on its own.

Both lineages write the same wire header for the same input, so their ASCII sets agree on the parity byte (51, 105, 27, 22, 43).

The two texts with non-ASCII characters are the cases that tell the lineages apart. The same Latin-1 sentence is carried as ISO-8859-1 without ECI by one lineage (parity 139) and as UTF-8 with ECI by the other (parity 8). The same Japanese sentence is carried as UTF-8 with ECI (parity 6) and as Kanji mode with no ECI (parity 176).

A decoder has to report whichever of these is on the wire, and a fixture set whose parity was computed over the wrong bytes would fail the gate. For that reason every repetition count in the corpus is odd, because an even repetition XORs to 0 in every charset. For the same reason the Latin-1 sentence carries an odd number of accented characters: with an even number, the ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8 parities coincide.

The third-party set (`zxing-cpp-samples/sample01`, 4 captures, version 15-L, parity 95, `PROVENANCE.md` and the Apache-2.0 `LICENSE` beside the files) is the one set this repository's tooling did not produce. Its symbols are grayscale photographs of about 267 px with no module matrix. They exercise the image path only, and every manifest field comes from the reader.

When the set was imported, this library's image decoder ended with `UnsupportedContent` on all four. Detection and error correction were therefore already sound, and only the mode indicator stood in the way.

The corpus also found one image-path defect unrelated to Structured Append. `codeglyphx/sixteen-symbols-max-v2-l-2of16` read through the matrix path but not from its PNG. The alignment pattern's ring and two data modules form a false finder, which the row scan confirms at 5 px/module and up. At the time, the finder selection scored module size alone. Every candidate measured the same size, so the selection preferred the false finder to the real bottom-left one.

The fix (2026-09-19) selects the finder triple by its shape (see the decoder spec's image detection lessons). The fixture now reads like every other, and `FinderPatternSelectionTest` renders it at 3 to 16 px/module.

**Sanity gate** (`StructuredAppendSanityGate`): every symbol is rendered and read with the pinned zxing-cpp reader before it is written. The gate checks that:

- index and count match the encoder's claim;
- version, ECC and mask match the manifest;
- the parity equals the XOR of the bytes the set actually carries (the reader's raw `Bytes`, concatenated in index order), and those bytes are one known encoding of the case text;
- the per-symbol texts, concatenated in index order, equal the case text. Where the encoder does not expose a symbol's text, the text is taken from the reader.

Fourteen sets passed on first generation once the `Net.Codecrete.QrCodeGenerator` pin moved from 3.1.0 to 3.2.1. Version 3.1.0 wrote parity 0 on every set, the defect that 3.2.0 fixed, and the gate is what caught it.

### Corpus contents (Micro QR, 23 cases × 2 lineages)

The cases cover every version × legal ECC combination (M1 detection-only, M2/M3 L+M, M4 L+M+Q) and every supported mode. They include capacity-boundary payloads (padding-free), short payloads (terminator + pad paths), and a UTF-8 byte-mode case. That case is in the qrtool lineage only, because libzint rejects UTF-8 input.

Both lineages share the case list (`MicroQRCorpus`): 17 fixtures come from zint-libzint and 23 from qrtool. The 5 Kanji cases are qrtool-only, because libzint emits Byte mode for the same input. They are at M3 and M4 only, the versions whose mode indicator is wide enough.

Version and ECC are pinned per case. The mask pattern in the manifest comes from the zxing-cpp READER during the sanity gate, so it too comes from an external implementation.

**Sanity gate**: every generated Micro QR fixture is rendered and decoded with the pinned zxing-cpp reader before it is written. Payload, version and ECC level must match the manifest, so a broken generator cannot poison the committed corpus.

### Corpus contents (rMQR, 108 zint-libzint + 44 qrtool cases)

The rMQR corpus was built in implementation-plan Phase 5.1a, BEFORE the tables, because its symbols are the oracle for the table tests. The two lineages carry different case lists (`RmQRCorpus`) on purpose:

- **zint-libzint** (ASCII-only): the systematic sweep. It has a single-character case for every one of the 32 versions × {Numeric `1`, Alphanumeric `A`, Byte `a`} (96). ECC alternates so that every version appears at both M and H, and the leading data codewords show the count-indicator width for each version × mode. Per-height capacity boundaries add 12 more: numeric max at M on the widest width, and byte max at H on the narrowest.
- **qrtool**: one capacity-boundary case per version with rotating mode / ECC (32), UTF-8 / Japanese byte-mode cases (4; libzint rejects non-ASCII) and Kanji-mode cases (8; libzint cannot emit Kanji at all). Four of the Kanji cases were added in Kanji encoding phase 6.6. The first four left some Kanji count widths to derivation, and the new four fill a version at each of those widths: 2 bits (R7x43-M, 3 characters), 3 (R7x59-M, 6; R9x43-H, 3) and 6 (R9x139-M, 38). All are under 11 modules high, so qrtool's tail defect does not touch them. One Kanji case, `r15x59-m-kanji-jisx0208-divergent`, carries exactly the seven Shift_JIS cells where JIS X 0208 and CP932 disagree. Its bytes are pinned on the case, because .NET cannot encode the JIS X 0208 readings. It is the fixture that fails if the decode table is ever rebuilt from CP932.

Neither lineage writes an ECI header. Payloads are fixed literals or fixed cyclic patterns. The tool keeps its own copy of the version / capacity table (`RmQRVersionTable`, values from [rMQR Encoder](rmqr-encoder.md)), so it never depends on the library it produces oracles for.

**Sanity gate** (`RmQRSanityGate`): every fixture is rendered and decoded with the pinned zxing-cpp reader before it is written. The payload is compared on raw bytes (`Bytes` vs `payloadUtf8Hex`), because the reader exposes UTF-8 without ECI with a legacy-charset guess in `Text`. `Extra("Version")` must equal `R{H}x{W}`, and `Extra("EcLevel")` must equal the manifest ECC. The reader's `DataMask` (4) is recorded.

Kanji fixtures are the exception to the raw-byte comparison. A Kanji segment puts the Shift_JIS bytes in `Bytes`, so for these fixtures the gate compares `Text` instead. That is the reader's JIS X 0208 reading, which is exactly what this library's decoder has to reproduce.

All 144 cases passed on first generation. The corpus has since grown to 152 with the Kanji cases.

### Consuming tests

`StandardQrFixtureTest` decodes every fixture twice, through the matrix path (`TryDecode(modules, size, …)`) and the image path (`TryDecode(SKBitmap, …)`). It asserts payload, version, ECC level and, on the matrix path, the generator's mask pattern.

`MicroQRFixtureTest` likewise exercises both the matrix path and the PNG image path (`MicroQRCodeDecoder.TryDecode(SKBitmap, …)`, Phase 4b). It also asserts zero corrected errors and, on the matrix path, the mask pattern taken from the reader.

`RmQrFixtureTest` (Phase 5.1a scaffolding) pins the shape of the rMQR corpus:

- both lineages;
- every version in both lineages and at both ECC levels;
- one single-character libzint case per version × mode;
- manifest ↔ matrix ↔ PNG consistency;
- structural invariants that do not depend on the tables (finder / sub-finder corners, edge timing rows).

Since Phase 6.4 it also decodes every fixture through the public matrix path and checks payload, version and ECC, with `ErrorsCorrected` 0 for libzint and ≤ 1 for the qrtool tail defect. It also re-decodes the module centers sampled from the PNG. Since Phase 7 it also decodes every PNG through the public image path (`RmQRCodeDecoder.TryDecode(SKBitmap, …)`, `Decode_PngFixture_*`), with the same payload / version / ECC / corrections expectations.

`KanjiFixtureTest` states the Kanji guarantee once, across all three symbologies. It decodes every Kanji fixture through both the matrix and the image path. It asserts a minimum Kanji case count per symbology, so a regeneration cannot silently drop them. It pins the divergent-cell fixture to its JIS X 0208 readings.

`KanjiEncoderOracleTest` (Kanji encoding phase 6.6) turns the same fixtures into an encoder oracle. A single Kanji segment at a fixed version and level has one valid stream. So this library's symbol of the same text, written with `AllowKanji` and with the mask pinned to the one the manifest records, must equal the fixture module for module, except for qrtool's rMQR tail modules. (The mask is pinned for Standard QR and Micro QR; rMQR has one mask.) The test also requires the Kanji fixtures to cover every Kanji count width (Standard QR 8, 10 and 12 bits; Micro QR 3 and 4; rMQR 2 to 7). It also requires the Kanji fixtures filled to capacity to hold exactly the count this library holds there. The divergent-cell fixture is the one Kanji fixture the test leaves out, by name, because its text is not one this library writes in Kanji mode.

The real images are measured by the sweep, not asserted as a set. Five Standard QR decode tests read the few images that a decoder change was built for, each at the right angles it reads:

- `KeystoneFrameDecodeTest`: five keystoned captures.
- `TwoAxisTiltDecodeTest`: `qrcode-2/fix-finderpattern-order`.
- `SpreadRingDecodeTest`: nine turns of captures whose rings are printed or read thin or thick.
- `ParallelogramCoverageDecodeTest`: `qrcode-2/qr-circles-1`.
- `SmallLatticeMeshDecodeTest`: `qrcode-3/22`.

`StructuredAppendFixtureTest` checks the Structured Append corpus in four ways:

- It decodes every Structured Append symbol through the matrix path (where a matrix exists) and the image path. It asserts the symbol's own text, version, ECC, mask, zero corrected codewords (matrix path, with the flipped-module negative control below) and the three header values.
- It decodes every matrix fixture into a one-character destination and requires the header to be absent from that failed result. This checks the "reported on success only" rule at the point where it is enforced.
- It pins the reassembly rules on the manifests themselves: one count and one parity per set, and indices 0..count-1 each present once.
- Like `KanjiFixtureTest`, it pins the corpus shapes a regeneration could silently drop: both encoder lineages and the captures, a 2-set and a 16-set, a Kanji-mode set, and a different parity per lineage for the two charset-divergent texts.

The encode direction has its own cross test, `StructuredAppendZXingCrossTest`. It covers nine sets written by `CreateStructuredAppend` (every charset, `Optimal`, boost, a BOM, the sixteen-symbol set). ZXing.Net reads each symbol in-process, and each symbol must carry the position, count, parity and text this library's decoder reports. The wider three-reader check with the native oracle is the `spot-check-structured-append` command.

Each fixture class also carries a **negative control** for its clean-decode corrections assertion. The same fixture with one data module flipped must decode with exactly one corrected codeword. Without the control, a dead `ErrorsCorrected` counter (always 0) would leave every zero-corrections assertion green while proving nothing. The control fails in that case.

The flipped module is the first codeword module in placement order. For Standard and Micro QR that is the bottom-right corner. For rMQR it is found by the placement zigzag over the naive function-module map. Micro QR excludes M1, which is detection-only and rejects any data damage. rMQR runs the control on the libzint lineage only, because qrtool has no zero-corrections baseline due to its tail defect.

### Regeneration

```bash
# qrtool binary (pinned version + SHA-256), one-time per machine:
pwsh tools/QRInteropFixtures/get-qrtool.ps1

dotnet run --project tools/QRInteropFixtures -- regenerate

# Structured Append sets only (also part of regenerate):
dotnet run --project tools/QRInteropFixtures -- regenerate-structured-append

# Third-party captures, never regenerated: re-import from a zxing-cpp checkout, recording its commit
dotnet run --project tools/QRInteropFixtures -- import-structured-append-samples <zxing-cpp-root> <commit>

# Structured Append encode interop: sets this library writes, read by the three pinned readers,
# parity compared with the pinned balancing encoder (findings in the oracle matrix)
dotnet run --project tools/QRInteropFixtures -- spot-check-structured-append

# Kanji encode interop: every encoder cell, ASCII \ and ~ beside Kanji runs, and a Kanji segment
# after ECI 26, read by every pinned reader of each symbology (findings in the oracle matrix)
dotnet run --project tools/QRInteropFixtures -- spot-check-kanji
```

The same tool also holds the oracle probes. They are run by hand, and their findings are recorded in the matrix below rather than asserted in CI, because they need the native oracle on the machine. The probes are:

- `spot-check-microqr`, `spot-check-rmqr` and `spot-check-structured-append`.
- `spot-check-kanji`: this library's Kanji output through every pinned reader (below).
- `probe-creator`, `probe-rmqr` and `probe-rmqr-capacity`.
- `probe-kanji`: which lineage can emit Kanji mode, per symbology.
- `probe-kanji-sweep`: every Kanji-mode cell through qrtool + zxing-cpp, diffed against CP932. It writes `kanji-sweep.tsv`.
- `generate-kanji-table`: emits the library's `ShiftJisKanjiTable` from that sweep. It refuses unless the data matches the published JIS X 0208 totals and its CP932 delta is exactly the seven documented cells.

`kanji-sweep.tsv` is committed alongside the tool, for three reasons. It is the provenance for a generated table that ships in `src/`. It carries the CP932 column that the divergence claim rests on. And with it committed, the table can be regenerated and reviewed without the native oracles on hand.

The tool wipes and rewrites each available generator's directory. Fixture updates must be committed as an explicit, reviewed change, because a generator-version bump that silently alters fixtures is exactly what the corpus is meant to catch.

### Image decode sweep

The fixtures above prove that a foreign symbol decodes from its matrix and from a clean render at 8 px/module. They say nothing about how the image decoders hold up as the image gets harder. Until 2026-09-21, every sweep that measured this drew this library's own symbols.

`tools/QRImageDecodeSweep` measures it against other readers, image for image. Its main number is the **gap**: images zxing-cpp reads and this library does not get through. The **reverse** is the opposite: images this library reads and zxing-cpp does not.

```bash
# Synthetic renders: every encoder's symbol of the same payload through the same render, 23 kinds
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/QRImageDecodeSweep -- sweep [qr|micro|rmqr|all] [cases] [outDir]

# The committed real images, each at the four right angles
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/QRImageDecodeSweep -- corpus [outDir]

# Two result files of the same run from two trees, image for image: gained, lost, and every lost image by name
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/QRImageDecodeSweep -- compare <before.csv> <after.csv>

# What a destination too short costs Micro QR and rMQR, render for render; and two such files from two trees
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/QRImageDecodeSweep -- destination [micro|rmqr|all] [count] [outDir]
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/QRImageDecodeSweep -- compare-destination <before.csv> <after.csv>

# Third-party images, never regenerated: re-import from a zxing-cpp checkout, recording its commit
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/QRImageDecodeSweep -- import-corpus <zxing-cpp-root> <commit>
```

- **Encoders**: this library, ZXing.Net, QRCoder, QrCodeGenerator, CodeGlyphX, libzint and qrtool for Standard QR; this library, libzint and qrtool for Micro QR and rMQR. A case fixes the payload, the level and the version, and every encoder gets the same case. The payload is ASCII, so that a failure is an image failure and not a character-set convention. Micro QR and rMQR pin the version in every encoder. Standard QR sizes the payload instead: longer than the version below holds, and no longer than the version asked for holds, so that the smallest version that fits is the one asked for. The first cut took 75-100 % of the version's capacity. From version 6 up, that also fits the version below, and 230 of 400 cases landed under their version (two at version 40, three at 39). Another encoder may still choose a neighbouring version through its own segmentation, which is part of what its symbols are. Each row carries the version its symbol has. The run prints the number of cases where this library's symbol does not land on the version asked for (zero). The first cut's error was a claim about the generator that nothing counted, and a claim about a sample is cheap to check.
- **Kinds**: the test suite's own renderers, linked from `tests/FeatherQR.Tests/Shared` (crisp nearest-neighbour and anti-aliased path at a fractional scale and random sub-pixel offset, supersampled at any rotation with and without keystone). Added to them are bilinear upscales, mip-mapped downscales, right-angle turns, mirrors, a JPEG round trip, and each library's own image writer. A kind measured here is a kind a test draws. This includes the four-module quiet zone the supersampled renderer draws round Micro QR and rMQR symbols, where the other kinds draw the two modules their specifications ask for. That zone is left as the rotation tests have it, and a wider quiet zone is within either specification.
- **Readers**: this library, zxing-cpp and ZXing.Net. Each is given the same grayscale buffer and told the symbology.
- **Pairing**: render parameters are seeded by arithmetic on the case and kind indices (never `GetHashCode`, which is randomized per process). Two runs therefore write byte-identical result files, and two trees can be compared render for render. A row's key is how its image was made, and beside the key the row carries a digest of the pixels. `compare` keeps a pair whose digests differ out of gained and lost, and lists it in a column of its own. If an encoder picks another mask or a renderer changes between the two trees, the pair is two different images, and a read that moved says nothing about the decoder. Every recorded table uses the default case counts (400 / 400 / 640: ten per Standard QR version, a hundred per Micro QR version, twenty per rMQR version).
- **Content is not gap**: if this library decodes an image into another text, or refuses its bit stream (`InvalidBitstream`, `UnsupportedContent`, `UnmappedCharacter`), the image was still located, sampled and error-corrected. Such an image is counted in its own column. In the real-image sets that column holds Byte-mode Shift_JIS without an ECI header (eleven images, which zxing-cpp reads by guessing the character set), one GS1 symbol, and one symbol whose bit stream is refused and which neither other reader reads.
- **A destination too short** (`destination`): each Micro QR and rMQR render is decoded into three destinations (a sized one, one a character short, and one of 2 characters). Each call is timed as the fastest of five rounds, and each round makes the three calls in turn.
  - The renders are 600 draws per symbology from a fixed seed: a random version, level and text, turned, 2 × 2 supersampled, with uniform noise. These are the sets behind the cost figures of the [single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan). A draw whose text no length fits is skipped, which leaves 577 Micro QR renders and 600 rMQR.
  - Until 2026-10-01 the rMQR draws counted versions from 0, which is not a version number. Those draws were dropped, and R17x139 was never drawn.
  - The set also holds the renders that the destination contract test draws with a finder-like pattern inside the symbol.
  - The summary lists the random renders version by version, with 0 for a version the set lacks. Each row carries a digest of the render's pixels.
- `compare-destination` pairs two trees' renders by name and, like `compare`, by that digest. It lists every status, version or text that moved within a pair whose two renders are the same image. It also lists the renders that are not the same image in both files. It reports the cost over the same-image pairs, and how many such pairs there were.
  - A file from before the digest (2026-10-01) is paired by how each render was made (kind, ppm, angle, noise). That detects a redrawn set, but not a changed renderer, and the comparison says so.
  - The times depend on the machine, so only their ratio to the sized call can be compared between runs.

The sweep is a measurement, run by hand. It needs the native oracles, and its result is a table to compare, not a condition to assert. Timings from 2026-09-27, without qrtool: a default `sweep all` takes about 40 s on 32 hardware threads, nearly all of it Standard QR (Micro QR and rMQR take a few seconds each), and `corpus` takes about a second.

A decoder change that moves reads is measured with the sweep against the commit before it, image for image, under these rules:

- **No misread.** A read returns the encoded text, over every sweep and the corpus. The baseline is zero.
- **Nothing lost silently.** Every lost render is listed by kind, and the reverse does not shrink without a stated reason.
- **Failure paths measured on failures.** The failure cost is timed on two-level and blurred noise, on a damaged symbol of each symbology and on another symbology's image. Each figure is the fastest of interleaved runs, reported beside the success-path benchmarks. A read that multiplies the cost of every unreadable image is a trade-off to state, not a side effect.
- **The finder's candidates on noise are pinned.** The candidate counts on the two-level noise set stay identical unless the change is to the finder. If it is, those counts are the change's headline number.
- **The corpus beside the sweep**, in every report. A change that moves the threshold or the sampled grid says so and takes a new baseline. Only speed work and refactors are held to results identical bit for bit.
- **The baseline built apart, and the corpus held by this library's columns.** The commit before is checked out with `git worktree add --detach`, and the sweep and the corpus run there, so nothing built from the tree being changed reaches the baseline. The sweep's result files are byte-identical from run to run. The corpus file is not: zxing-cpp's column moved on 9 of 624 rows, all at rotation 0, with this library unchanged (2026-09-29). A refactor is held to the columns this library writes, which are the ones `compare` counts.

Before anything is built, each failing render is sampled through the geometry it was drawn with, and that matrix is decoded. This is the true-transform column. A render that then reads failed in the frame (finder centres, dimension, perspective). One that does not read failed in the pixels (threshold, where a module is sampled). The sweep knows every render's geometry, so the column is cheap. For grey edges below 2 px/module, and for keystone in both Standard QR and rMQR, it pointed at the frame first.

The change then owes the test suite a render of the failing class with its drawn corners asserted, and the negative the repair must not admit (the same class with its data destroyed). Each must go red with the repair removed. Every new bound or gate must fail a test when moved. A guard that neither a sweep nor a test can tell from its absence is deleted.

The encoder does not decide whether a symbol reads. Over the first sweep's 135,000 decodes, a kind's read rate differed between encoders by at most 10 of 400 cases. That difference is mask choice: 40 to 50 % of QrCodeGenerator's, libzint's and qrtool's matrices differ from this library's, against 6 % of ZXing.Net's and 1.5 % of QRCoder's and CodeGlyphX's. Every library's own image writer read 100 %. The encoder columns stay, because a failure that does not move with the render is the encoder's (qrtool's R17x43, below).

#### Where the gap stands

Measured 2026-09-28 on `main` at 8ba2178, with the default cases and six Standard QR encoders (qrtool was not on the machine). The per-kind table is in the Standard QR record's envelope. The Micro QR and rMQR records list the kinds under 99 %.

| Synthetic renders | This library | zxing-cpp | ZXing.Net | Gap | Reverse |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard QR, 54,400 | 52,327 | 48,738 | 32,545 | 18 | 3,607 |
| Micro QR, 18,400 | 17,887 | 12,524 | | 0 | 5,363 |
| rMQR, 29,440 | 28,656 | 7,771 | | 0 | 20,885 |

On the first baseline (2026-09-21, seven encoders, payloads sized as above), the Standard QR gap was 2,002 renders. Of these, 1,907 were in five kinds: anti-aliased edges at 1.25-2 px/module, bilinear upscales at 1.5-2, any rotation at 2-3 and keystone at 6-20 %. The 18 left are anti-aliased renders at 1.0-1.25 px/module, below this library's envelope. There zxing-cpp reads 41 of 2,400, and this library 356.

Micro QR and rMQR had a gap of a few renders per kind, plus 54 in Micro QR bilinear upscales at 2-2.5 px/module. zxing-cpp reads far fewer of both symbologies, so they are tracked by their own read rate.

The real images, each at four right angles:

| Set | Images | This library | zxing-cpp | ZXing.Net | Gap | Reverse | Content |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `qrcode-1` | 8 | 32/32 | 32 | 24 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `qrcode-2` | 56 | 148/224 | 201 | 100 | 16 | 7 | 52 |
| `qrcode-3` | 18 | 67/72 | 72 | 56 | 5 | 0 | 0 |
| `qrcode-4` | 24 | 54/96 | 60 | 64 | 7 | 1 | 0 |
| `qrcode-5` | 16 | 64/64 | 64 | 64 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `qrcode-6` | 15 | 60/60 | 60 | 60 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **Standard QR** | 137 | **425/548** | 489 | 368 | **28** | 8 | 52 |
| `microqrcode-1` | 16 | 64/64 | 59 | | 0 | 5 | |
| `rmqrcode-1` | 3 | 12/12 | 12 | | 0 | 0 | |

On the first run this library read 295 of the 548 Standard QR images (gap 153) and 60 of the 64 Micro QR ones. The largest cause was a shading gradient across the symbol, which one global threshold splits into two solid halves (42 of the 43 gap reads in `qrcode-5` and `qrcode-1`). The regional pass reads them ([image decode passes](qrcode-symbologies.md#image-decode-passes)). Each image left in the gap has a recorded cause:

- **Out of scope** (12 reads). `qrcode-2/#940` and `qr-model-1` are Model 1 symbols (zxing-cpp reports `]Q0`). Their format word reads under Model 1's mask, and their data, placed as Model 1 places it, fails. `#258` draws its finder rings as dots. Its diagonals read only with each run moved by 0.52 to 0.68 of a module, which is past the half-module bound.
- **The grid** (14). `high-res-1` is a version 34 on curled paper at 2.2 px/module. Its mesh interior reads, and the bands along its edges have about half their function modules wrong. `qrcode-4/29` is on curved paper, and no alignment pattern is found. Of 3,721 fourth anchors within 3 modules, 12 read, none with fewer than 15 corrections (20 through zxing-cpp's corners). `qrcode-3/03` is binarized with heavy ink spread, and the anchors that read need 23 or 24 corrections. `qrcode-4/12` at 0° and 90° has all four corners within 0.12 module of zxing-cpp's plane: a knife edge.
- **A finder at its floor** (2). `qrcode-3/30` at 270° has diagonals at the 2 px floor. `qrcode-4/15` at 270° has a falling diagonal rounded at one outer corner (runs of 5, 5, 15, 5 and 2 px).

Putting the Kanji segment first does not help either: before the ECI, zxing-cpp reads its bytes as ISO-8859-1. Its `Content::switchEncoding` drops every charset a mode set once the symbol has an ECI (a Kanji segment sets Shift_JIS that way). Bytes ahead of the first ECI default to ISO-8859-1. So a symbol with an ECI anywhere loses its Kanji segments. All four readers read the same segment with no ECI, which is what this library writes. This decided against writing Kanji beside an ECI header. ISO/IEC 18004:2015 is on zxing-cpp's side (an ECI governs the bytes of every mode), and readers are split on it, so Kanji beside an ECI header is never written (2026-10-01). The same day, checked by hand, the iPhone Camera app (iOS 26.5) read all six phone-test symbols as written (Kanji with no ECI, ECI 26 over UTF-8 alone, and the four ECI 26 and Kanji arrangements). It reads Kanji as JIS X 0208 whatever the ECI. An Android 17 phone's own QR scanner and Google Lens read none of the Kanji symbols, but did read ECI 26 UTF-8. This is why Kanji mode is written only on request ([When Kanji mode is written](qrcode-symbologies.md#when-kanji-mode-is-written)) |
| BoofCV (Java) | decode | decode | - | claimed | Candidate additional decode oracle; not evaluated |

Independence caveat: ZXing.Net and zxing-cpp descend from the same ZXing lineage, so they count as one independent implementation family, not two. Zint and the Rust crates are separate lineages. zxing-cpp's READER and the libzint WRITER ship in one native binary, but they are algorithmically independent codebases. A round trip that creates and then reads a symbol within that binary therefore still exercises two lineages.

rMQR correction capacity (`probe-rmqr-capacity`, 2026-08-21): zxing-cpp corrects rMQR at full Reed-Solomon strength, with no reserved misdecode-protection codewords `p`. The question was whether rMQR reserves `p` the way ISO/IEC 18004 Table 9 does for Micro QR. ISO/IEC 23941 Table 8's capacity column is paywalled, so this was measured against zxing-cpp instead.

For each of the 64 version × ECC combinations, the probe damages a symbol one module at a time. It keeps only flips that this library's decoder reports as exactly one more corrected codeword. The damage therefore saturates at this library's capacity in every Reed-Solomon block, without consulting a block-structure table. The probe then checks zxing-cpp in both directions:

- It must still decode at saturation. Otherwise it stops below this library, which would mean a reserved `p` that this library ignores.
- It must not decode one error past saturation. Otherwise it reaches further, which would mean this library's capacity is too low.

All 64 agree, and every saturation count equals `blocks × ⌊ecc per block / 2⌋` exactly. This is evidence from the reference implementation, not a reading of the standard. The Correction cap decision in [rMQR Decoder](rmqr-decoder.md) stays open until someone reads Table 8.

Oracle scarcity, decode direction: zxing-cpp is the only maintained OSS decoder for Micro QR and rMQR. ZXing Java/.NET, rqrr (Rust) and gozxing (Go) do not read them, and BoofCV (Java) reads Micro QR only. Encoder verification therefore rests on one external decode lineage, plus specification-derived vectors and the in-repo extraction tests. This is a structural limit, not a tooling gap. The decode direction has no such limit: multiple independent encoder lineages (zint, Rust qrcode2) generate the fixture corpus that exercises this library's decoder.

Toolchain policy: oracles must be pinned and obtainable without fragile, environment-dependent builds. NuGet packages and prebuilt static binaries qualify. Building C++/Python toolchains on dev machines or CI does not. Rust tools qualify through prebuilt release binaries. Under this policy the fixture generators for Phase 3 are libzint (via the pinned ZXingCpp package) and qrtool (prebuilt binary, pinned by version + checksum). Docker-pinned builds remain a fallback.

## Why

### Why the corpus sits where it does among the test layers

The corpus is one of four test layers. Each layer exists because it catches a failure mode the others cannot see.

- **Module-matrix conformance** is the primary oracle: fixed matrices with pinned masks, compared before any image is involved. It is the only layer that can fail when the encoder and the decoder agree on the same wrong interpretation. No round-trip test can detect that, by construction.
- **This corpus** covers external symbol → this library's decoder. The counterpart, this library's encoder → external decoder, is a separate direction and is tested separately. A single round trip through one external tool proves neither half on its own.
- **Image degradation** tests exercise detection and sampling deterministically (rotation, blur, noise, perspective). They use symbols whose matrix the layers above have already shown to be good.
- **Physical scanners** are acceptance, never proof. A phone that fails to read a spec-conformant symbol is an interoperability fact, not a specification violation. It can inform a decision but must never gate one. This is why no physical test suite exists (see the scope table in [qrcode-symbologies.md](qrcode-symbologies.md#scope-decisions)).

Two structural rules follow.

**Sampling and payload decoding need a testable boundary between them**. The matrix-level decoder entry points exist partly for this reason. They let an image failure be traced to "sampled the wrong matrix" or "decoded the right matrix wrongly", instead of being one opaque false.

The other rule is that **the coverage cross-product has to be cut deliberately**. Version × mode × ECC × payload × degradation is unbounded. So matrix-level conformance is exhaustive, while payload and degradation coverage focuses on boundaries. Anything larger is left to manual runs rather than pull-request CI.

### Why ZXing.Net is the first generator

ZXing.Net is already a pinned test dependency, runs in-process, and needs no external toolchain. So the harness (manifest schema, loader, writer, tests, CI wiring) could be built and proven against the shipped Standard QR implementation at once. The plug-in generator interface (`IFixtureGenerator`) exists so that Zint / qrtool / zxing-cpp can be added for Micro QR and rMQR without touching the harness.

### Why fixtures assert the decode direction only

Two conformant encoders may legitimately produce different final matrices, because mask selection and mode segmentation are implementation choices, not normative outputs. Matrix equality against an external fixture is therefore **not** a valid encoder-conformance test. The corpus verifies this library's *decoder* against external symbols. This library's *encoder* is verified by external decoders (ZXing.Net cross tests today, zxing-cpp in interop CI later). For Micro QR / rMQR it is also verified by spec-derived matrix tests, where the manifest pins the mask.

### Why fixtures are committed rather than generated in CI

Committed fixtures keep PR CI self-contained and deterministic (no Rust/C++/Python toolchains). They also turn fixture drift into a reviewable diff, instead of a silent side effect of a dependency upgrade.

## Lessons learned

- ZXing.Net's `ZXing.QrCode.Internal.Encoder` (rather than the public `BarcodeWriter`) returns the core `ByteMatrix` plus version, mode, and **mask pattern**. The mask lets fixture tests assert that this library's format-information decode reproduces the generator's mask choice exactly. That is a much stronger check than payload equality alone.
- For Micro QR the equivalent mask metadata comes from the zxing-cpp READER during the sanity gate (`Extra("DataMask")`), not from the encoders. Neither libzint (through the wrapper) nor qrtool reports its mask choice. Metadata from the reader is just as external, and it also proves the value is on the wire.
- qrtool's `--type ascii` output (two characters per module) makes extracting the fixture matrix exact and image-free. But trailing light modules are trimmed from each line, so the parser must pad them back. `--mode` requires an explicit `--symbol-version`.
- Regenerating fixtures on Windows rewrites working-copy files with LF endings. When the content is unchanged, the only diff is line-ending churn (`git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` is empty). Restore such no-op rewrites rather than commit them.
- The public `QRCodeWriter.encode` path scales and pads to a requested pixel size, so extracting the core matrix from it is lossy. Generating from the internal encoder and rendering the PNGs in the tool keeps the matrix and the image pixel-exact for a known quiet zone and module size.
- ZXing's encoder honors the requested ECC (it never downgrades it), so the manifest can record the requested level as the expected decode result without reading it back from the symbol.
- A committed external symbol is not automatically a byte-exact oracle. qrtool's rMQR output carries a systematic tail defect (the last h − 10 placement modules are never written) that zxing-cpp corrects silently. The sanity gate (payload + metadata equality) therefore passed 36/36, while the encoder-side final-message comparison found 12 mismatches. Where the reader can correct errors, agreement across lineages decides: libzint is byte-exact, qrtool differs only in the last codeword's low bits, and both are consistent with the ISO codeword counts that qrtool's layout could not even hold. The corpus keeps the qrtool symbols as real-world "one corrupted ECC codeword" decoder cases, with the defect documented, rather than dropping them.
- qrtool 0.13.2 has a second rMQR defect, and this one is not correctable. R17x43 at level M comes out with about 88 modules different from libzint's and this library's matrices, which agree byte for byte, and no reader decodes it. Level H of the same version carries only the tail defect. The image decode sweep found it as ten cases failing in every render kind, the library's own 8 px/module writer included. A failure that does not move with the render is the encoder's. The sweep leaves R17x43 out of the qrtool lineage.
- libzint's creator in the pinned ZXingCpp package dies with an access violation on some payloads, some of the time. Standard QR case 301 of the sweep (523 byte-mode characters at level Q) kills it about one run in three, in a process that does nothing else.
  - It was first taken for a threading fault, because the first crashes came while readers ran on other threads, and a serial scan of the same cases passed. Then a lock changed nothing, a run with a collector thread forcing finalizers changed nothing, and finally a serial pass crashed on the same case.
  - A managed process cannot catch the crash. So the sweep runs the creator in a worker process, retries the case the worker died on, and gives a case up only after eight deaths in a row.
  - That makes a dropped case rare but not impossible, so a drop is never silent. The case gets a row saying so, the table lists it as not produced, and the run exits with a failure, because its images are no longer the set other runs have.
  - The fixture generator has not hit the crash (its payloads are short). But a new long-payload libzint case should be generated more than once before it is trusted.
  - A worker killed this way can linger and hold its files. Build to another output directory rather than wait for it.
- The zxing-cpp sample sets are small, because that repository recompressed them (240 px WebP for most photographs). All eight sets are 1.1 MB, so they are committed rather than fetched.
- **Failing classes found with one's own renders grow by one a sweep; a gap to another reader closes.** Before the sweep, each round drew this library's symbols, found a failing class and fixed it. Nothing showed whether the decoder had got better or the tests easier. The gap cannot be moved by changing a test. It shows where the decoder is behind, not merely where it is imperfect, and it has an end: zero, or a residual with a cause.
- **A corpus someone else collected finds the class nobody here drew.** The synthetic kinds came from failure classes this project already knew, so none of them drew a lighting gradient. That was the largest cause on photographs: the real-image gap was 28 % of the Standard QR reads, against 3 % in the sweep. ZXing.Net, behind in every synthetic kind, at first read more photographs than this library (368 against 295), with the hybrid binarizer that the regional pass now uses. A class the corpus shows once can also be much larger when drawn. One bent version 7 photograph became a set of bowed renders with a gap of about 1,200 in 1,400.
- **A stand-in renderer is checked against the world before a test trusts it.** The uneven-lighting renderer's first shadow depth (75 % across a three-module edge) was picked to make this library fail. At that depth every reader measured reads only some directions (zxing-cpp and ZXing.Net 2 of 8), and at 85 % no reader reads any direction. Pinned in a test, it would have been a target nothing meets.
- **The oracle's column belongs to its run.** zxing-cpp's reads of the corpus moved by one to three between runs of one build. In one of three runs of one build on 2026-09-28, it read 17 fewer Standard QR images, 16 of them at 0° (472 against 489), while this library's columns were identical in all three. Its native reader also died once with an access violation in `ZXing_ReadBarcodes`, and the rerun was clean. Compare this library's columns between trees, and take the oracle's from more than one run.
- **A brute-force reader needs a time budget.** CodeGlyphX's reader, used in the keystone and Micro QR comparisons, spent over 25 CPU-seconds per image on keystoned renders and never finished a cell. So it is run with a stated budget (1 s), and its column is what it reads in that time. Stopping one cell's process did not stop the loop over cells: the next cell ran without a budget beside the timing runs and doubled their times.
- **The expected texts must reach the tool as committed.** The corpus's `.txt` files are marked `-text` in `.gitattributes`. But a checkout older than that line keeps CRLF working copies (autocrlf) until the files are written again. Every reader's read of a multi-line text is then graded as another text. This hit 16 `qrcode-5` reads, and zxing-cpp's four reads of `high-res-1`, which kept that image out of the gap and out of its triage. `git ls-files --eol` shows such files as `i/lf w/crlf`. Delete them and check them out again.
- **A premise holds per case, or the case tests nothing.** When the destination tests of the two single-finder decoders became one contract test (`DestinationContractTest`, 2026-10-01), every case was given the premise its rule needs. rMQR's case "another symbol that fits is still read", with the small symbol drawn first, then failed its premise. The small symbol had been tried first and read, so the case had passed whatever the rule did. Drawn at 4 px/module against the big symbol's 6, the small symbol is now tried second in both orders.
- **A fault planted at one grid site can be masked by the next site.** One fault let a read that does not fit go on at one site of a Micro QR candidate. It cost only a few grids where a later site of the same candidate read the symbol again and ended it, and no timing bound catches that. Planting the fault and timing a set of renders found, for each site that had no render, one that reads only at that site. These cost about 27, 30 to 38 and 53 times a sized call through the timing frame, the module boundaries and the coverage re-read (per-call medians, 2026-10-02). A fault still not caught is recorded with the reason the code gives ([single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan)).
- **Every place a candidate ends is a fault to plant.** The first list planted one fault per rule. That covered 7 of Micro QR's 9 places that return on a terminal result, and 4 of rMQR's 13. Planting at every such place found more faults that nothing caught, some costing tens of times a sized call. Each was then either caught by a render that reads through it, or recorded with the code's reason (2026-10-02).
- **Moving a rule into shared code moves its planted fault too.** Micro QR's per-size and turned site faults had been caught through the coverage re-read that the site let run. Once the gate that refuses a re-read after a read that does not fit moved into `GridRead`, its fault was planted, and caught, there for both decoders. The site faults are still caught, through what the candidate's later grids read.
- **A render built to read one way is read the way the decoder samples it.** A Micro QR render was drawn so that its grid failed when sampled at the module centres and read when read by coverage (`TwoTextRenderer`, the data inverted under each centre). It still read with both of Micro QR's coverage conditions switched off. Another grid of the decoder read it with no re-read. A test of a read made one way is shown to go red with that way removed.
- **A worst case over a render set moves between runs of one tree.**
  - With a call timed several times in a row, the worst one-character-short ratio of the 577 Micro QR `destination` renders was 1.05, 1.10, 1.25 and up to 1.50 in runs of one tree. It was a different render each time, while the median held.
  - With the three calls taken in turn each round, nine runs gave a median of 1.00 and a 95th percentile of 1.01 to 1.03. The worst moved from 1.02 to 1.46, a different render each run (2026-10-01 and 02).
  - So a comparison checks the median and the 95th percentile, and checks the worst only against its spread.
- **A draw that throws is a draw the set does not have.** The rMQR `destination` set cast `random.Next(32)` to a version numbered from 1. The 0 it drew made the generator throw. The generator skips a draw no text fits, and the largest version went missing unnoticed. A set states what it holds, version by version, before its figures are used, and a draw skips only a text that does not fit. The `destination` draw catches only the generator's error for such a text. The sweep's cases size their text with `TryGetRequiredBufferSize`, so an out-of-range version or level stops the run. The sweep's cases had caught every exception: an rMQR level drawn out of range gave 322 of the 640 cases a one-character text, and the run finished.
- **A timing test compares calls, not loops.** If a loop of sized calls is timed and then a loop of short ones, one stall of the machine lands in one loop and moves the ratio. If the calls are taken in turn and compared by their medians, a stall lands in one call, which moves neither median.
- **`tools/mutation_check.cs` refuses a file with changes of its own,** since `git checkout` would not restore it. A change's own files are checked with `--allow-dirty`. They are copied aside first, and checksums after the run confirm the copies match. A line repeated elsewhere in its file is found together with the line beside it, with a `␤` in the fault's text standing for the line break.
- **A published table is a second reading, not an oracle.** The Wikipedia transcription of ISO/IEC 23941 Table 3 agrees with all 128 of rMQR's count widths. Its Table 7 agrees with the Kanji capacity those widths give on 63 of 64 cells. The 64th, R11x77-M, is a corrupt row holding R11x59-H's Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte cells. The Kanji widths 2, 3 and 6 rested on that reading and on derivation until qrtool's fixtures tested them on real symbols.
- **An oracle that does not write what is asked about can still build it.** No pinned encoder writes a Kanji segment after ECI 26. But QrCodeGenerator 3.x takes explicit segments, which gave `spot-check-kanji` that symbol without reaching into this library's internals, and with a Kanji table that is not this library's.
- **A reader check has to confirm what it is reading.** The first texts holding ASCII `\` and `~` beside kanji were short. In Standard QR and Micro QR they came out UTF-8, since a Kanji plan did not lower the version. They read back correctly and proved nothing about Kanji plans. The check now requires zxing-cpp's raw bytes to be the text's Shift_JIS encoding, and each symbology to carry both characters in a Kanji plan.
- **An image reader's miss can be about finding the symbol.** ZXing.Net's one miss in the Kanji spot check was a 27-L image it found only with the pure-barcode hint. The tool retries with the hint and reports how often it had to, so a detection miss is not counted as a misread cell.
